1.q: הַ⁠דָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֣ה אֶֽל־יִרְמְיָ֔הוּ מֵ⁠אֵ֥ת יְהוָ֖ה לֵ⁠אמֹֽר
1.note: Jeremiah is using the expression **The word that was to Jeremiah from Yahweh** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Jeremiah is using the word **saying** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. This also occurs in verses 5 and 11.

1.q: הַ⁠דָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֣ה אֶֽל־יִרְמְיָ֔הוּ מֵ⁠אֵ֥ת יְהוָ֖ה
1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [7:1](ta:07).

2.q: ק֥וּם וְ⁠יָרַדְתָּ֖ בֵּ֣ית הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֑ר וְ⁠שָׁ֖מָּ⁠ה אַשְׁמִֽיעֲ⁠ךָ֥ אֶת דְּבָרָֽ⁠י
2.note: Here, **and there** marks **I will cause you to hear my words** as the goal or purpose of **Arise and go down to the house of the potter**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh would cause Jeremiah to hear his words]

3.q: וָ⁠אֵרֵ֖ד בֵּ֣ית הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֑ר ו⁠הנ⁠הו עֹשֶׂ֥ה מְלָאכָ֖ה עַל הָ⁠אָבְנָֽיִם
3.note: This event happened after Yahweh told Jeremiah to go down to the potter’s house. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [After that, I went down to the house of the potter, and behold, he was doing work on the wheels]

Jeremiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look]

Here Jeremiah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

4.q: וְ⁠נִשְׁחַ֣ת הַ⁠כְּלִ֗י אֲשֶׁ֨ר ה֥וּא עֹשֶׂ֛ה בַּ⁠חֹ֖מֶר בְּ⁠יַ֣ד הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֑ר וְ⁠שָׁ֗ב וַֽ⁠יַּעֲשֵׂ֨⁠הוּ֙ כְּלִ֣י אַחֵ֔ר כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָשַׁ֛ר בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֖ר לַ⁠עֲשֽׂוֹת
4.note: This event happened after the vessel **was ruined**. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [And the vessel that he was making with the clay was ruined in the hand of the potter, so then he made it into another vessel, as it was right in the eyes of the potter to make]

4.q: וְ⁠נִשְׁחַ֣ת הַ⁠כְּלִ֗י אֲשֶׁ֨ר ה֥וּא עֹשֶׂ֛ה בַּ⁠חֹ֖מֶר בְּ⁠יַ֣ד הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֑ר
4.note: The expression **was ruined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Something ruined the vessel that the potter was making with the clay in his hand]

Here, **the hand of the potter** represents the potter’s control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verse 6. Alternate translation: [under the potter’s control]

Jeremiah is using **he returned and made it** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he made it again.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he made it again into another vessel]

Jeremiah is using **in the eyes of the potter** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the potter’s judgment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the potter judged it best]

5.note: See how you translated this expression in 1:4.
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:9.

6.q: לֹא אוּכַ֨ל לַ⁠עֲשׂ֥וֹת לָ⁠כֶ֛ם בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל
6.note: Yahweh is using the question form to affirm that he has complete authority over the people of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am certainly able to do to you, house of Israel!]
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8.

6.q: הִנֵּ֤ה כַ⁠חֹ֨מֶר֙ בְּ⁠יַ֣ד הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֔ר כֵּן אַתֶּ֥ם בְּ⁠יָדִ֖⁠י בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
6.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that just as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so the house of Israel is in his hand]

6.q: כַ⁠חֹ֨מֶר֙ בְּ⁠יַ֣ד הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֔ר כֵּן אַתֶּ֥ם בְּ⁠יָדִ֖⁠י
6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the clay** is entirely under the control of **the potter**, so the people of Israel are entirely under Yahweh’s control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as the potter shapes the clay however he wishes, so I can do with you whatever I wish]
Here, **my hand** represents my control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my power]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:26.

7.q: רֶ֣גַע אֲדַבֵּ֔ר עַל גּ֖וֹי וְ⁠עַל מַמְלָכָ֑ה לִ⁠נְת֥וֹשׁ וְ⁠לִ⁠נְת֖וֹץ וּֽ⁠לְ⁠הַאֲבִֽיד
7.note: Here, the word **to** marks **to uproot and to tear down and to destroy** as the goal or purpose of Yahweh’s speaking **concerning a nation or concerning a kingdom**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Yahweh is presenting a possible condition. He will only do what he describes in the next verse if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. This also occurs in verse 9. Alternate translation: [If it ever happens that I speak concerning a nation]

Here Yahweh is speaking of destroying a nation as if it were a plant that he could **uproot** and a building that he could **tear down**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [or concerning a kingdom, to overthrow it and to bring it down and to destroy it]

The terms **to uproot**, **to tear down**, and **to destroy** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [or concerning a kingdom, to utterly demolish it]

8.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible condition. He will only **relent concerning the disaster** if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [and if it should happen that that nation turns from its evil]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a nation changing its behavior as if it **turns** away from a direction in which it had been traveling. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and if that nation abandons its evil behavior]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from doing what is evil]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **disaster**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the harmful things]

9.q: וְ⁠רֶ֣גַע אֲדַבֵּ֔ר עַל גּ֖וֹי וְ⁠עַל מַמְלָכָ֑ה לִ⁠בְנֹ֖ת וְ⁠לִ⁠נְטֹֽעַ
9.note: Here, the word **to** marks **to build and to plant** as the goal or purpose of Yahweh’s speaking **concerning a nation or concerning a kingdom**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Here Yahweh is speaking of establishing a nation as if it were a house that he could **build** and a crop that he could **plant**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to establish it and make it prosper]

The terms **to build** and **to plant** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to cause it to flourish]

10.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible condition. He will only **relent concerning the good** if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [But if that nation should do what is evil in my eyes]

Yahweh is using **in my eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in my judgment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what is evil in my judgment]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how I said I would treat it well]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:23. This also occurs in verse 19.

11.q: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה הִנֵּ֨ה אָנֹכִ֜י יוֹצֵ֤ר עֲלֵי⁠כֶם֙ רָעָ֔ה
11.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that he himself is forming evil against you]

Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus the attention of the men of Judah and the dwellers of Jerusalem on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Here Yahweh is speaking of planning calamity as if he were a potter **forming** a vessel out of clay. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I am preparing calamity against you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a plan**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I will do]

Yahweh is using **a man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each man” or “each person.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each man]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a person’s conduct as if it were a **way** along which that person walks. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each man from his evil behavior]
See how you translated this expression in 7:3.

12.note: Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between what he tells the people to do and how they respond. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Instead of obeying, they will say, “It is hopeless]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [But they will say that it is hopeless because they will walk after their own plans]

The people are using **we will walk after our own plans** as a common expression of the culture to mean “we will do whatever we ourselves decide to do.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we will follow our own intentions]

Here the masculine term **each man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and each of us will do the stubbornness of our own evil heart]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and each man, because of the stubbornness of his evil heart, we will do evil]

The people are speaking of themselves in the third person as **each man**, even though they continue in the first person with **we will do**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this consistently in the first person. Alternate translation: [and each of us, the stubbornness of our own evil hearts, we will do]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:17. This also occurs in verse 12.

13.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why Yahweh says]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that no one has ever heard of anything like what his people have done. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one has ever heard things like these!]

Yahweh is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were a young unmarried woman, **The virgin of Israel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The nation of Israel]

14.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the snow on the mountains of Lebanon never disappears. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The snow of Lebanon never leaves the rock of the field!]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

14.q: אִם יִנָּתְשׁ֗וּ מַ֛יִם זָרִ֥ים קָרִ֖ים נוֹזְלִֽים
14.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the cold mountain streams never stop flowing. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The foreign, cold, flowing waters are never removed!]

The expression **removed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [does anything remove the foreign, cold, flowing waters]

15.note: Yahweh uses the word **Yet** here to indicate a contrast between the constancy of the natural world and the unfaithfulness of his people. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But, unlike the constancy of the waters of Lebanon, my people have forgotten me]

Here, **worthlessness** represents worthless idols. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they burn incense to worthless idols]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people’s conduct as if it were a path along which they could **stumble**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they have failed to follow their ancient way of life]

In the clause **they have caused themselves to stumble**, the word **themselves** indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same people fill two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [and my people have willfully departed from the ways I set before them]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the faithful way of life that his people once followed as if it were **the paths of old**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the faithful life their ancestors lived]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people’s sinful conduct as if it were **a way not being built up**, that is, a rough track that no one has prepared for travel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to conduct themselves sinfully, in a way that no one has prepared]

The expression **not being built up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a way that no one has built up]

16.q: לָ⁠שׂ֥וּם אַרְצָ֛⁠ם לְ⁠שַׁמָּ֖ה שרוקת עוֹלָ֑ם כֹּ֚ל עוֹבֵ֣ר עָלֶ֔י⁠הָ יִשֹּׁ֖ם וְ⁠יָנִ֥יד בְּ⁠רֹאשֽׁ⁠וֹ
16.note: Here, the word **to** marks **to make their land a desolation** as the goal or purpose of the actions that Yahweh describes in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

The terms **a desolation** and **a hissing** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a permanent object of horror]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [desolate]

The **hissing** referred to here was a symbolic action by which people showed contempt and horror at what had happened to a place. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [a place about which people will always hiss to show their contempt]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific person. He means travelers in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Anyone who passes by it]

To **shake his head** was a symbolic action by which a person showed shock and scorn at what he saw. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [will shake his head to show his shock and scorn]

Here the masculine term **his** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [will shake his or her head]

17.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a wind of the east** drives dust and chaff away before it, so Yahweh will drive his people away in every direction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As an east wind drives away dust, so I will scatter them]

Here, **the face** represents the presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the presence of the enemy]

Yahweh is using **The neck and not the face I will show them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will turn away from them and refuse to help them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will turn my back on them and refuse to help them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **calamity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when they suffer terrible things]

18.note: Jeremiah is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Here Jeremiah is introducing his opponents as new participants in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And some people who opposed me said]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **perish**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [the priests will always be able to teach the law]

18.q: כִּי֩ לֹא תֹאבַ֨ד תּוֹרָ֜ה מִ⁠כֹּהֵ֗ן וְ⁠עֵצָה֙ מֵֽ⁠חָכָ֔ם וְ⁠דָבָ֖ר מִ⁠נָּבִ֑יא
18.note: These three clauses mean basically the same thing. Jeremiah’s opponents are repeating the same idea with different words in order to emphasize it. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [for we will always have someone to tell us what God requires]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [nor will the wise stop advising us]

Jeremiah’s opponents are using the adjective **wise** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [from the wise man]

Here, **the tongue** represents what people say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and let us attack him with our words]

19.note: Here, **the voice** represents the words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [listen to the words of my opponents]

20.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to protest that it is wrong for people to repay good with evil. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [People should not repay good with evil!]

The expression **be repaid** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Should someone repay evil in place of good]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil** and **good**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [Should someone act harmfully in return for acting kindly]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of his opponents’ plot to kill him as if they had **dug a pit** in which to trap an animal. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have plotted secretly to kill me]
See how you translated this phrase in 7:10.

The pronoun **them** refers to the people who are now plotting against Jeremiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to speak good concerning these people who now oppose me]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s anger were something moving toward the people that Yahweh could **turn back**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to turn your anger away from them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your being angry]

21.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why I want you to give]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:30.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **famine**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to starve]

Jeremiah is speaking of **the sword** as if it were a living thing that could seize people with its **hands**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power of those who wield swords]

Jeremiah is saying what he wants to happen to **their wives**. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [And may their wives become bereaved of children and widows]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And let their wives become bereaved of children and let their wives become widows]

Jeremiah is using **those killed of death** as a common expression of the culture to mean “those who die from a deadly disease.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who die from a deadly disease]

Jeremiah is saying what he wants to happen to **their men**. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [and I want their men to be killed by deadly disease]

The expression **those killed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [those whom the plague kills]

The expression **struck** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and their young men whom enemies struck with the sword]
Here, **the sword** represents warfare. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [struck down by weapons of war]

22.note: Jeremiah is saying what he wants to happen in the houses of his opponents. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [May a cry be heard from their houses]

The expression **be heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let people hear a cry]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a cry**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people crying out]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [since]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of his opponents’ plans to destroy him as if they had **dug a pit** in which to trap an animal. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have secretly plotted to seize me]

Here, the word **to** marks **to capture me** as the goal or purpose of digging **a pit**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that they can capture me]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of his opponents’ schemes to harm him as if they were **traps** hidden along a path where he would walk. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they have secretly prepared ways to destroy me]

23.note: Jeremiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between forgiving his opponents and defeating them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [rather than forgiving them, make them stumble]
